title: 04 — Azure Fundamentals for .NET Developers
html:
04 — Azure Fundamentals for .NET Developers

The platform concepts you need before any service makes sense: the resource hierarchy, regions, RBAC, IaC, networking, and cost.

1. The resource hierarchy

Microsoft Entra tenant  (one identity boundary for your organisation)
│
└── Management group(s)          ← policy and RBAC applied here cascade down
    └── Subscription             ← BILLING boundary + quota boundary
        └── Resource group       ← LIFECYCLE boundary (deploy/delete together)
            └── Resource         ← app service, storage account, SQL database…
Level What it's for Key facts
Tenant Identity. One Entra directory A subscription trusts exactly one tenant
Management group Apply policy/RBAC across many subscriptions Up to 6 levels; useful once you have >3 subscriptions
Subscription Billing, quotas, isolation ⚠️ Quotas are per subscription per region — the usual cause of "cannot create resource: quota exceeded"
Resource group A container with a shared lifecycle Resources can talk across RGs; the RG is only a management boundary. Deleting an RG deletes everything in it
Resource The thing itself Has a globally unique ARM resource ID

Subscription strategy — the usual pattern:

sub-myapp-prod      ← production only. Tight RBAC, budget alerts, change control
sub-myapp-nonprod   ← dev + test + UAT
sub-platform        ← shared services: DNS, ACR, log analytics, hub network

💡 Separate production into its own subscription. It gives you a hard blast-radius boundary, independent quotas, unambiguous cost attribution, and a natural place to apply stricter policy.

Resource group strategy: group by application + environment + lifecycle, not by resource type. rg-myapp-prod-uksouth containing the app, its database, its storage and its Key Vault is right. rg-all-databases is wrong — you can't delete or move an application cleanly.

1.1 Naming conventions

Adopt the CAF (Cloud Adoption Framework) abbreviations and be consistent — you will read these names in alerts at 3am.

<type>-<workload>-<environment>-<region>[-<instance>]

rg-shop-prod-uksouth            resource group
app-shop-api-prod-uksouth       app service
asp-shop-prod-uksouth           app service plan
func-shop-overlap-prod          function app
sql-shop-prod-uksouth           logical SQL server
sqldb-shop-main-prod            database
st shop prod uksouth  →  stshopproduksouth   ⚠️ storage: lowercase alphanumeric only, 3–24 chars
kv-shop-prod-uks                key vault (3–24 chars, globally unique)
sb-shop-prod-uksouth            service bus namespace
cr shop prod  →  crshopprod     container registry (alphanumeric only)
id-shop-api-prod                user-assigned managed identity

⚠️ Some names are globally unique across all of Azure: storage accounts, Key Vaults, App Service default hostnames, Container Registries, Service Bus namespaces, Cosmos accounts. Others are unique only within the resource group. Plan for this — kv-payments is long gone.

1.2 Tags

tags: {
  environment: 'production'
  application:  'shop'
  owner:        'platform-team@example.com'
  costCentre:   'CC-4471'
  dataClass:    'confidential'
  managedBy:    'bicep'
}

💡 Enforce required tags with Azure Policy (deny or modify effect). Without enforcement, tagging decays within a quarter and you can never answer "what is this £8,000 costing us for?".

2. Regions, availability zones, and pairs

Concept Meaning Design implication
Region A geographic area with one or more datacentres Choose for latency to users, data residency, and service availability (not every service is in every region)
Availability Zone Physically separate datacentres within a region, independent power/cooling/network Zone-redundant deployment survives a datacentre failure. Usually a small cost premium — take it in production
Region pair A paired region for platform-managed replication and staged updates Geo-redundant storage replicates here; Azure avoids updating both simultaneously

Design guidance:

  • Multi-AZ (zone-redundant) by default in production. It's cheap insurance. Set zoneRedundant: true on App Service plans (Premium v3+), use ZRS storage, zone-redundant SQL and Service Bus Premium.
  • Multi-region only when the business pays for it. Active-active multi-region means solving data consistency across regions — a 10× complexity step, not a checkbox. Active-passive with a documented RTO is usually the right compromise.
  • ⚠️ Egress costs money and cross-region traffic is slow. Keep chatty components in one region. Data transfer into Azure is generally free; out is not.

3. Azure RBAC

Security principal  ×  Role definition  ×  Scope   =   Role assignment
(user, group,          (set of allowed      (MG / subscription /
 service principal,     actions)             RG / individual resource)
 managed identity)

Built-in roles you'll actually use:

Role Grants
Owner Everything, including granting access. ⚠️ Very few people
Contributor Manage resources, but cannot grant access
Reader View only
User Access Administrator Manage access only
Storage Blob Data Contributor / Reader Data-plane access to blobs
Key Vault Secrets User / Officer Read secrets / manage secrets
Azure Service Bus Data Sender / Receiver Send / receive messages
AcrPull / AcrPush Pull / push container images
Website Contributor Manage App Service

⚠️ The control plane / data plane distinction is the single most confusing thing about Azure RBAC. Contributor on a storage account lets you manage the account (change tiers, read the access keys) but does not by itself grant Storage Blob Data Contributor, which is what your code needs to read a blob using Entra authentication. People routinely grant Contributor, find their app still gets 403, and reach for access keys instead of adding the correct data role. Don't.

Rules:

  • Assign to groups, not users. Individual assignments become unmanageable and outlive the person's need for them.
  • Assign at the narrowest scope that works — resource group, not subscription.
  • Prefer built-in roles; create custom roles only when nothing fits, and keep them few.
  • Use PIM (Privileged Identity Management) for standing admin access — just-in-time elevation with approval and audit 🔄 (Entra ID P2).
  • Deny assignments exist but are mostly used by Azure itself (blueprints, managed apps).
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/rg-shop-prod/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stshopprod"

⚠️ RBAC changes can take a few minutes to propagate. A newly granted role that "doesn't work" is often just not propagated yet — and a cached token still carries the old claims until it expires.

4. Infrastructure as Code with Bicep

Bicep is a DSL that transpiles to ARM JSON. It's the Azure-native option; Terraform is the multi-cloud option. Both are fine — pick one per organisation.

// main.bicep
targetScope = 'resourceGroup'

@description('Environment: dev, test, or prod')
@allowed(['dev', 'test', 'prod'])
param environment string

param location string = resourceGroup().location

@description('Deployed automatically by CI; used for tagging')
param buildNumber string = ''

var namePrefix = 'shop-${environment}'
var isProd = environment == 'prod'

var commonTags = {
  environment: environment
  application: 'shop'
  managedBy: 'bicep'
  build: buildNumber
}

// ── Log Analytics + Application Insights ───────────────────────────────
resource logs 'Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces@2023-09-01' = {
  name: 'log-${namePrefix}'
  location: location
  tags: commonTags
  properties: {
    retentionInDays: isProd ? 90 : 30
    sku: { name: 'PerGB2018' }
  }
}

resource appInsights 'Microsoft.Insights/components@2020-02-02' = {
  name: 'appi-${namePrefix}'
  location: location
  tags: commonTags
  kind: 'web'
  properties: {
    Application_Type: 'web'
    WorkspaceResourceId: logs.id          // workspace-based (classic is retired)
  }
}

// ── App Service ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
resource plan 'Microsoft.Web/serverfarms@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'asp-${namePrefix}'
  location: location
  tags: commonTags
  sku: {
    name: isProd ? 'P1v3' : 'B1'
    capacity: isProd ? 2 : 1
  }
  properties: {
    reserved: true                        // Linux
    zoneRedundant: isProd                 // survive a datacentre failure
  }
}

resource api 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'app-${namePrefix}-api'
  location: location
  tags: commonTags
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' }    // ← managed identity, no secrets
  properties: {
    serverFarmId: plan.id
    httpsOnly: true
    siteConfig: {
      linuxFxVersion: 'DOTNETCORE|10.0'
      alwaysOn: isProd
      http20Enabled: true
      minTlsVersion: '1.2'
      ftpsState: 'Disabled'
      healthCheckPath: '/health/ready'
      appSettings: [
        { name: 'ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT', value: environment == 'prod' ? 'Production' : 'Development' }
        { name: 'APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING', value: appInsights.properties.ConnectionString }
        { name: 'KeyVaultUri', value: vault.properties.vaultUri }
      ]
    }
  }
}

resource stagingSlot 'Microsoft.Web/sites/slots@2023-12-01' = if (isProd) {
  parent: api
  name: 'staging'
  location: location
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' }    // ⚠️ the slot has its OWN identity — grant it too
  properties: { serverFarmId: plan.id, siteConfig: { linuxFxVersion: 'DOTNETCORE|10.0' } }
}

// ── Key Vault + RBAC for the app's managed identity ────────────────────
resource vault 'Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults@2023-07-01' = {
  name: 'kv-shop-${environment}'
  location: location
  tags: commonTags
  properties: {
    tenantId: subscription().tenantId
    sku: { family: 'A', name: 'standard' }
    enableRbacAuthorization: true         // 💡 RBAC, not legacy access policies
    enableSoftDelete: true
    softDeleteRetentionInDays: 90
    enablePurgeProtection: isProd ? true : null   // ⚠️ irreversible once enabled
  }
}

var keyVaultSecretsUser = '4633458b-17de-408a-b874-0445c86b69e6'   // built-in role GUID

resource vaultAccess 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments@2022-04-01' = {
  scope: vault
  name: guid(vault.id, api.id, keyVaultSecretsUser)   // deterministic → idempotent
  properties: {
    principalId: api.identity.principalId
    roleDefinitionId: subscriptionResourceId('Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions', keyVaultSecretsUser)
    principalType: 'ServicePrincipal'
  }
}

output apiHostname string = api.properties.defaultHostName
output apiPrincipalId string = api.identity.principalId

# Deploy — always preview first
az deployment group what-if -g rg-shop-prod -f main.bicep -p environment=prod
az deployment group create  -g rg-shop-prod -f main.bicep -p environment=prod

Bicep practices that matter:

Practice Why
what-if before every apply, and put its output in the PR The plan is the review artifact
Modules for reusable components module api 'modules/app-service.bicep' = { ... }
guid() for role-assignment names Deterministic → the deployment is idempotent
Parameterise by environment, don't fork the file One template, three parameter files
Never mutate resources in the portal Drift makes the next deployment destructive
Deployment mode: Incremental (default) Complete mode deletes anything not in the template ⚠️
Store outputs, not secrets ⚠️ Deployment outputs are readable in the deployment history — never output a secret

Terraform equivalent considerations: remote state with locking (Azure Storage + blob lease), terraform plan in the PR, apply on merge, prevent_destroy on production data resources, and separate state files per environment.

5. Networking essentials for a .NET developer

You don't need to be a network engineer, but you need these five concepts:

Concept What it is When it bites you
VNet + subnet Private address space; subnets segment it Address-space overlap between VNets you later need to peer
NSG Subnet/NIC-level firewall rules The reason your app can't reach the database
Private Endpoint A private IP for a PaaS service inside your VNet ⚠️ Requires private DNS or the name still resolves to the public IP
VNet integration (App Service) Outbound traffic from the app goes through your VNet Needed to reach private endpoints or on-prem
Service Endpoint Restricts a PaaS service to specific subnets (traffic stays on the Azure backbone but keeps a public IP) Simpler than Private Endpoint; less isolation 
Internet → Front Door/App Gateway (WAF) → App Service (public inbound)
                                              │ VNet integration (outbound)
                                              ▼
                                     Subnet ──► Private Endpoint ──► Azure SQL
                                                (10.0.2.4)            (public access disabled)

⚠️ The single most common private-endpoint failure: DNS. The FQDN sql-shop-prod.database.windows.net must resolve to the private IP. That requires a Private DNS Zone (privatelink.database.windows.net) linked to the VNet, plus the app resolving through Azure DNS. Symptoms: works from a VM in the VNet, times out from the App Service, or connects but over the public endpoint.

Outbound IPs: App Service has a set of possible outbound IPs that can change when you scale or change tier. If a partner firewall allow-lists your IP, use a NAT Gateway with a static public IP instead of listing App Service outbound IPs 🔄.

6. Cost management

The mental model: you pay for provisioned capacity (App Service plan, SQL vCores, VM), consumption (Functions executions, storage transactions, bandwidth), and egress.

Lever Impact
Right-size from metrics, not fear The most common waste is a P2v3 plan running at 8% CPU
Reserved instances / savings plans 30–60% off the steady baseline for a 1- or 3-year commitment
Dev/test subscriptions Discounted rates; and auto-shutdown non-prod outside working hours
Azure Hybrid Benefit Reuse on-prem Windows/SQL licences
Storage lifecycle policies Auto-tier to cool/cold/archive; delete old blobs
Log Analytics retention and sampling ⚠️ Frequently a top-3 line item. Sample telemetry; set retention per table
Egress Keep chatty components co-located; use CDN for repeat downloads
Budgets and anomaly alerts Alert at 50/80/100% of budget, and on unusual spikes
Tags + cost analysis You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute

⚠️ The classic surprise bills: Log Analytics/Application Insights ingestion, Cosmos DB provisioned RUs left at a load-test setting, an orphaned public IP or premium disk after deleting a VM, cross-region data transfer, and a Consumption Function stuck in a retry loop.

🧪

az consumption usage list --top 20 --query "[].{name:instanceName, cost:pretaxCost}" -o table

7. The Well-Architected Framework (the five pillars)

Worth knowing by name — Microsoft documentation and architecture reviews use this vocabulary.

Pillar The question it asks Practical checks
Reliability Does it stay up and recover? Multi-AZ, health checks, retries with backoff, tested backups, defined RTO/RPO
Security Is it protected? Managed identity, least privilege, private networking, encryption, Defender for Cloud
Cost optimisation Are we paying for what we need? Right-sizing, reservations, lifecycle policies, budgets
Operational excellence Can we run it? IaC, CI/CD, monitoring, runbooks, blameless postmortems
Performance efficiency Does it scale? Autoscale rules, caching, async, load tested at 2× peak

💡 Run the Azure Well-Architected Review assessment against a workload once a year. It's free, structured, and generates a prioritised list you can actually action.

8. Governance

Tool Purpose
Azure Policy Enforce or audit rules: allowed regions, required tags, deny public IPs, require HTTPS, deny storage account keys
Initiatives Groups of policies (e.g. a CIS or ISO benchmark)
Management groups Apply policy/RBAC across subscriptions
Resource locks CanNotDelete / ReadOnly — ⚠️ a lock on a resource group blocks deletion of everything inside, including from your IaC pipeline
Defender for Cloud Security posture score, recommendations, threat detection
Activity log Who did what to which resource, and when. The first place to look after an unexpected change

💡 The three policies worth applying on day one: required tags, allowed locations, and deny storage accounts with public blob access.

9. The Azure SDK for .NET — patterns that apply to every service

Modern Azure.* packages share one design, so learning it once covers Storage, Key Vault, Service Bus, Cosmos, and the rest.

// 1. DefaultAzureCredential — the same code works locally and in Azure.
//    Chain: environment vars → workload identity → managed identity →
//           Visual Studio → Azure CLI → Azure PowerShell → interactive browser
builder.Services.AddSingleton<TokenCredential>(new DefaultAzureCredential(
    new DefaultAzureCredentialOptions
    {
        // In production, exclude the developer credentials — they add latency
        // on every probe and can silently pick the wrong identity.
        ExcludeVisualStudioCredential = true,
        ExcludeAzurePowerShellCredential = true,
        ManagedIdentityClientId = builder.Configuration["UserAssignedIdentityClientId"]  // if user-assigned
    }));

// 2. Register clients through Microsoft.Extensions.Azure — handles lifetime,
//    pooling, retries, and logging correctly.
builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.AddBlobServiceClient(new Uri($"https://{account}.blob.core.windows.net"));
    clients.AddSecretClient(new Uri(vaultUri));
    clients.AddServiceBusClientWithNamespace($"{ns}.servicebus.windows.net");
    clients.UseCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential());

    clients.ConfigureDefaults(options =>
    {
        options.Retry.Mode = RetryMode.Exponential;
        options.Retry.MaxRetries = 3;
        options.Retry.Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200);
        options.Retry.MaxDelay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);
        options.Retry.NetworkTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
    });
});

Rules for every Azure SDK client:

  1. Clients are thread-safe and expensive to create — register them as singletons. Creating a BlobServiceClient per request is the same class of bug as new HttpClient().
  2. The SDKs retry transient failures by default — don't add your own retry loop on top, or you multiply the attempts.
  3. Always pass a CancellationToken.
  4. DefaultAzureCredential caches tokens and refreshes them automatically. Don't cache the token yourself.
  5. ⚠️ DefaultAzureCredential in production should exclude the developer credentials. Each excluded probe saves latency at startup and removes a class of "it authenticated as the wrong identity" confusion.

10. Checklist

  • Production in its own subscription, with budget alerts
  • Resource groups scoped per application + environment
  • CAF naming convention applied consistently
  • Required tags enforced by Azure Policy
  • Zone-redundant deployment in production
  • RBAC at the narrowest scope, assigned to groups; data-plane roles granted, not just Contributor
  • All infrastructure in Bicep/Terraform in the repo; what-if/plan reviewed in the PR
  • No manual portal changes to production resources
  • Managed identity on every service; zero connection strings with keys
  • Private endpoints where required, with the private DNS zone linked
  • Azure SDK clients registered as singletons with configured retry and timeout
  • Diagnostic settings sending logs to Log Analytics
  • Budgets, anomaly alerts, and a monthly cost review

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Difference between a subscription and a resource group? Billing/quota boundary vs lifecycle/management boundary.
  • Control plane vs data plane RBAC? Managing the resource vs accessing the data in it. Contributor on a storage account doesn't let your code read a blob via Entra auth.
  • How do you deploy infrastructure safely? IaC in the repo, what-if in the PR, apply on merge, no manual changes, incremental mode, deterministic role-assignment GUIDs.
  • What is DefaultAzureCredential and why is it useful? One credential chain that resolves to a developer identity locally and a managed identity in Azure — the same code, no secrets.
  • Why did my app get 403 on Key Vault after I gave it Contributor? Contributor is control plane; it needs Key Vault Secrets User on the data plane (with RBAC authorisation enabled).
